title: Overwatch's New Omnic Hero Shion Has a Human Face—and Fans Have Questions
summary: Overwatch's next season drops next week, and with it comes Shion, a new Omnic damage hero who leads the Hashimoto clan. She's a stylish gunslinger who can ride and launch a motorcycle at foes, and her distorted, intimidating voice sets her apart from more stoic Omnics like Zenyatta. But the moment her design was revealed, a familiar criticism resurfaced: her face looks strikingly human—and strikingly similar to other female heroes. Unlike the overtly robotic, somewhat featureless faces of Zenyatta or Ramattra, Shion has a human-like visage with the signature Omnic dots relegated to her forehead. This immediately drew comparisons to Anran, a hero released earlier this year who was blasted for resembling Kiriko and Juno. Fans have long speculated that Blizzard gives multiple female characters conventionally attractive, similar faces to boost sales of cosmetic skins—a theory that's hard to shake when you see side-by-side images. However, the outcry isn't unanimous this time. Some players note that Shion actually has a distinct nose, unlike the 'button nose' shared by Juno and Kiriko. 'Shion actually has a different nose for once omg,' tweeted one relieved fan. It's a small victory, but it highlights how closely the community scrutinizes each new face. Beyond the aesthetics, Shion's design raises compelling lore questions. In Overwatch's world, tensions between humans and Omnics have been a central theme, most prominently in the now-canceled campaign storyline. Why would an Omnic leader, who clearly doesn't shy away from attention, choose to look human? Does she harbor a self-hating complex, or is she trying to bridge a divide? If Blizzard leans into that narrative, it could transform a controversial design into a fascinating character study. The studio has been praised for its recent storytelling, so there's hope that Shion's appearance is more than skin-deep. Still, it's hard not to wonder if a bolder, less conventionally attractive design was left on the cutting room floor in favor of marketability. As one fan put it, 'a braver, less skin-sale-friendly design was lost in the process.' With Shion set to be a major player in season 3, we may soon get answers. Until then, she's already sparked a conversation about representation, design philosophy, and what we really want from our robot heroes.
why_it_matters: Video games aren't just about winning matches—they're stories and characters you connect with. When a game keeps recycling the same faces, it can make you feel like your identity isn't represented, and it raises questions about whether artistry or profit is driving the choices. As you grow into tomorrow's game designers or critics, your voice can push for bolder, more diverse creations.

background_read: Overwatch is a team-based shooter game released in 2016 by Blizzard Entertainment (a game developer famous for World of Warcraft and Diablo). In its story, robots called Omnics were created to help humanity, but later many turned hostile in a war called the Omnic Crisis. Some Omnics, like the monk Zenyatta, seek peace; others, like Ramattra, are militant.

A recurring complaint from the community is that many of Overwatch’s female heroes—such as Kiriko, Juno, and Anran—share very similar facial features, especially a small 'button nose' and soft features. Fans have made side-by-side image comparisons that spread widely online, fueling debates about whether Blizzard prioritizes selling cosmetic skins over diverse art.

The Omnic storyline was a major part of a planned single-player campaign that Blizzard later canceled, leaving many questions about human-robot tensions unanswered. Shion's release in season 3 could be an attempt to reignite that narrative, or simply a way to introduce a flashy new character with a motorcycle-riding ability.

NUANCE: The criticism isn't unanimous; some players note Shion has a distinct nose, a small victory that highlights how closely the community watches each design.

perspectives.description: Fans who noticed Shion's slightly different nose see it as progress, however tiny. They hope Blizzard is paying more attention and that this Omnic's human-like face will tie into a deep, well-written story about identity and acceptance.

Many long-time players feel Blizzard keeps prioritizing conventionally pretty faces to sell cosmetic skins, especially after Anran's similar controversy. They argue this makes the game's world less imaginative and alienates players who want to see themselves reflected in robot and human designs alike.

Across the gaming industry, female characters often face a 'same-face' problem, where a narrow idea of attractiveness overrides unique art. Overwatch's struggle mirrors a wider challenge for studios: balancing creative vision with the business reality that attractive characters sell more skins.

Shion's narrative arc could redefine what it means to be an Omnic, tackling themes of assimilation and self-hatred. If Blizzard commits to that story, it might silence critics and set a new standard for how hero-based games handle identity. Future hero designs might then be judged not just on looks, but on the depth they bring to the world.
